title: The Lotus Opens
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 21 of 40
content:
Iroh gave me a key wrapped in a tea receipt.

I unfolded the paper at the back counter, beneath a lantern that needed dusting. The key was brass, its teeth a little crooked. The receipt listed two tins of jasmine, a bag of dried citrus peel, and something in Iroh's tidy handwriting that looked suspiciously like *do not leave kettle unattended*.

"Is this a bill?" I asked.

"That depends. How expensive is your company?"

"Very."

"Then I am fortunate to have saved so carefully."

The city was just waking. Cart wheels clicked over the paving outside. Someone was calling the price of morning buns, and the Jasmine Dragon smelled of hot water, wood polish, and leaves I still couldn't identify by sight.

I tried the key in the side door. It caught halfway, then turned with a small reluctant scrape.

"It works," I said.

"With patience."

"It needs a locksmith."

Iroh looked wounded. "A locksmith is merely a man who has lost faith in persuasion."

Mina came through the kitchen carrying an empty tea tin and heard the last part.

"He's been persuading that lock for six months," she told me. "Don't let him tell you otherwise."

She took the receipt, read the note, and gave Iroh a look that could have emptied an army camp.

"You're giving Jasper the upstairs key?"

"That was the intention."

"And the rota?"

He blinked.

"The actual hours somebody will be paid to open, close and clean the shop?"

I laughed before I could stop myself. Mina didn't.

Iroh put his cup down.

"Ah."

"Exactly," she said. "A key doesn't mean free staff. Or somebody to stay late whenever a customer wants another story about the Dragon of the West."

He watched her go back to the kitchen, looking as though he had been soundly defeated.

"She likes you," I said.

"She likes a properly kept shop. I am a constant inconvenience."

"I can believe that."

We put the key on the counter between us. I had wanted one. I liked the thought of being able to come home from a Threadway crossing without knocking like a stranger. But it was strange how much fear could fit around a small piece of metal.

"What's it for?" I asked.

"The rooms above the shop, and the side entrance."

"Not the stockroom?"

"Not the stockroom."

"Not a promise I'll be here every morning?"

He looked at me for a longer moment. "No."

I touched the receipt with one fingertip. "Are you sure? Because I like being here. I also have other places and people in my life. I've been clear that I'm ethically non-monogamous and that I prefer polyamory. I don't want a key to become a quiet way of promising you I'll stop leaving."

Iroh leaned back against the counter. There was a tiny fleck of flour on his sleeve. He had somehow acquired it without going anywhere near the morning buns.

"I had hoped," he admitted, "that you would be glad to have a place to return to."

"I am."

"And I had hoped you might return often."

"I think I will."

He nodded, still watching the key.

"I see the difference," he said.

"Do you?"

"Yes." His expression turned wry. "Knowing it does not prevent an old man from being afraid of an empty room."

I thought of the chair by the window. He kept it in exactly the wrong place for somebody trying to carry a mop through the shop. I had been wanting to ask him about it for days.

"I can't promise you'll never miss me," I said.

"Nor should you."

"But I can tell you when I'm leaving, when I expect to be back, and when the plan changes. You can tell me if you need something without making me guess."

His fingers covered the receipt. "A guest is welcomed. A companion is consulted."

"That sounds like something you've rehearsed."

"Does it?"

"Extensively."

He looked delighted. Then Mina shouted that somebody had put a broken jar back on the shelf instead of recording it in the inventory, and the philosopher vanished.

By the time we reached the kitchen, half the citrus peel had spilled across the floor. The jar wasn't shattered, only cracked, but the lid no longer sealed. Iroh began gathering up the pieces as though he could personally apologize to every leaf.

"Those can't go back into the tea," Mina said.

"Of course not."

"I mean it."

"I heard you the first time."

"Then put the broom down and find the damaged-stock sheet."

I helped sweep while Iroh searched the stack of invoices. Mina checked the remaining jars and drew a small mark beside the supplier's name. She would ask for the replacement cost when the cart came back through the market.

I was useful. It felt good. Then the thought arrived, sharp and unwelcome: if I became useful enough, perhaps the key would start to belong to the job instead of the life.

I set the broom aside.

"Mina, if I work here on a regular shift, I'd like us to agree to hours. I don't want to be an emergency person who happens to sleep upstairs."

She regarded me for a moment, then smiled.

"Good. I already have one of those."

Iroh looked up from the invoices. "I appear to be losing this battle on every front."

"You're losing a battle with a cracked jar," Mina said. "Nobody else is fighting."

A customer arrived before we finished. An older porter, his cap pulled low against the morning wind, asked for hot water rather than tea. He recognized Iroh when he turned around.

For a moment neither man spoke.

"I knew you from the war," the porter said.

Iroh's face changed. Not much. His shoulders drew back, and the soft amusement went out of his eyes.

"I remember many people from that time," he answered.

"Not all of them remember you kindly."

I went still with the broom in my hand.

"I would not expect them to," Iroh said.

The porter looked at him for another long moment. Then he asked Mina the price of hot water. She gave it to him, and he paid. Iroh did not offer a speech, an apology to a stranger on behalf of a city, or a cup of tea that would make the exchange disappear.

The porter sat near the door where he could see the street. He drank slowly and left without saying goodbye.

Only after he was gone did I notice that Iroh had been holding the empty kettle for several minutes.

"Would you like to sit down?" I asked.

"No. There is work."

"That wasn't my question."

He set the kettle down with a soft thud.

For once he didn't have a clever reply.

We sat at the small table by the kitchen window. He could hear Mina speaking with a supplier outside. The shop wasn't waiting for him to become wise again; it was carrying on around him.

"I used to think," he said, "that there would come a morning when the war had stopped following me."

I reached for his hand and stopped just short of touching it. He turned his palm upward.

"I don't know how that morning would look," I said.

"Neither do I."

"I don't need you to tell me it was all for a reason."

"Good," he said. "It was not."

The words were quiet and hard. I kept holding his hand.

He told me one ordinary thing about Lu Ten: the way his son had eaten the soft center of a bun and tried to hide the crust beneath a plate. Iroh laughed once, surprised by the memory. Then the laugh broke, and he wiped his face with the back of his free hand.

I didn't try to repair the moment. I was learning that sitting beside someone could be loving without becoming an answer.

After a while, Mina brought in a fresh kettle and two cups. She put them down without commenting on our faces.

"Your schedule," she said to me. "Write down the shifts you actually want. I'll tell you what I can pay."

Then she turned to Iroh.

"And call a locksmith."

He sighed.

"I shall consider it."

"You'll call one."

"Very well."

I couldn't help laughing. He looked at me, mock-offended, and the corner of his mouth lifted.

The rest of the afternoon belonged to the shop. I carried cups. Mina counted stock. Iroh made a dreadful joke about a tea leaf that had traveled farther than most generals, and a customer politely pretended not to understand it. By evening my feet hurt, and the side-door key had warmed in my pocket.

When we closed, Iroh asked whether I wanted supper upstairs.

"Yes," I said. "Not because I have the key. Because I want to."

"An important distinction."

"You can make a joke now."

"I would never waste such a moment."

He bought two sweet buns on the way upstairs and dropped one while trying to open the door. We stood on the landing staring at it.

"An omen," he said gravely.

"Of what?"

"That I should have bought three."

I laughed until my eyes watered.

Inside, we ate the surviving bun and a bowl of rice. The window let in the smell of rain beginning on the stone street. He talked about a customer who had insisted his least expensive blend was his finest, and I told him Mina had already corrected three of his entries in the ledger.

"Only three?" he asked. "I am improving."

"At an alarming rate."

He leaned closer. "You know, I would like to kiss you."

"That's fortunate."

"Is it?"

"Very. Because I've been staring at your mouth for most of supper."

His face warmed. He reached for my hand, paused, and let me come the rest of the distance. We knocked the empty bowl sideways and had to rescue it before kissing properly. It was tender and rather ridiculous, and he laughed quietly against my cheek.

Later I put the spare key on the little hook beside the door. We closed the curtains and kept the rest of the evening to ourselves.

In the morning the shop would open whether I was there or not. Mina had a rota, the supplier had a claim for a cracked jar, and somewhere in Ba Sing Se a porter had memories that tea would not erase.

I could come back with the key.

I could also leave.

Iroh knew both things, and when I reached for his hand again he met me halfway.
